Database systems / 08 OF 08

ClubSphere

The last seat is a transaction.

A university club and event management system with student, coordinator, and admin workflows for membership, booking, waitlists, attendance, feedback, and reports.

See it in motion ↓Source ↗

01 / THE QUESTION

What needed to work?

Event capacity, role permissions, and waitlist order need to hold even when several users act on the same records.

Student, coordinator and administrator workflows backed by nine normalized MySQL tables, database integrity rules and transaction-based booking.

02 / THE DEMONSTRATION

Follow the idea through.

IN-MEMORY BOOKING EXPLANATION

Fill both seats, add a waitlisted student, and cancel the first booking.

03 / THE ENGINEERING

The decision behind it.

Use row-locked booking transactions and atomic FIFO promotion. Seat availability and promotion belong in the same transaction.

  1. 01Role-based workflows
  2. 02Booking transactions
  3. 03FIFO waitlist promotion
  4. 04Reports & integrity checks
  • Developed student, coordinator, and admin workflows for membership, booking, attendance, feedback, and reports.
  • Designed nine normalized MySQL tables with keys, constraints, and indexes.
  • Added two views, two stored procedures, and six integrity triggers.
  • Implemented row-locked booking transactions, atomic FIFO waitlist promotion, Argon2id password hashing, and server-enforced role and ownership checks.

04 / THE EVIDENCE

What the work demonstrates.

The original application uses row-locked booking transactions. This two-seat browser sketch illustrates seat allocation and promotion with fictional students.

The implementation supports membership, booking, waitlists, attendance, feedback and reports. Its recorded interfaces demonstrate different roles over real database records.

BOUNDARY OF THE EVIDENCE

The screenshots use demonstration accounts. The portfolio’s two-seat booking interaction is an in-memory explanation, not a connection to the MySQL service.
